newsitem.title: USA: Prudential's property unit downgraded by A.M. Best.
newsitem.headline: Prudential's property unit downgraded by A.M. Best.

text.p: A.M. Best said it downgraded the claims-paying ability rating of Prudential Insurance Co of America's main property-casualty unit to B++ from A-.
The move reflects the group's continued poor operating earnings, ongoing earnings volatility and above-average catastrophe risk, A.M. Best said.
The downgrade applies to Prudential Property and Casualty Insurance Co and its three reinsured affiliates, A.M. Best said.

A.M. Best said it does not expect meaningful positive returns until 1998, largely due to PRUPAC's five to 10 point loss ratio disadvantage to its national peers as well as expense drain stemming from systems investments and constrained premium growth from tightened underwriting standards.

A.M. Best said is encouraged that PRUPAC's most recent corrective actions, begun this spring under current management, have shown early signs of improved underwriting trends within its downsized personal lines book.

Nonetheless, PRUPAC's weak but improving earnings, combined with its above-average susceptibility to catastrophe losses, have led to PRUPAC falling below Best's "A-" profitability standards for an unacceptably long period, with sizable pretax operating losses generated over the past six years, A.M. Best said.

PRUPAC's poor 1996 operating results, with a six-month combined ratio of 114, and PRUPAC's financial projections for the next several years, led the insurance rating agency to believe PRUPAC will not achieve operating returns commensurate with A.M. Best's A- profitability standard in the near term.
A combined ratio measures an insurer's profitability.
Despite the downgrade, PRUPAC's B++ rating falls within A.M. Best's "secure" range, A.M. Best said.

The rating reflects the group's much-improved balance sheet strength and risk profile, reduced underwriting leverage, and substantial catastrophe mitigation progress in Florida, California and the Northeast, A.M. Best.
A.M. Best also said it is encouraged by Prudential's commitment to PRUPAC's new management team, which plans a number of marketing, distribution and operational initiatives.

Those initiatives will bring much greater underwriting discipline and market focus to the property/casualty unit, A.M. Best said, and such initiatives are necessary for PRUPAC to become a profitable, self-sufficient unit.
The "secure" rating also acknowledges the strength and financial flexibility afforded by its parent, Prudential Insurance Co of America.

Prudential showed its strong support of PRUPAC with its $725 million capital infusion into the property/casualty unit in 1992 -- equating to 125% of its surplus -- to offset huge Hurricane Andrew losses in that year.
PRUPAC, with $1.3 billion of net writings supported by $664 million of surplus at year-end 1995, ranks among the top 15 personal lines groups in the country.
